newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia bond yields stay lower, debate next move.
newsitem.headline: Australia bond yields stay lower, debate next move.

text.p: *Australian bonds yields were lower in the wake of the 1/2 point official rate cut, but the reaction has been relatively subdued with only the timing of the move being the surprise.
*Analysts now debating whether this cut is the last.
Australian bonds yields were lower in the wake of the 1/2 point official interest rate cut, but the reaction has been relatively subdued with only the timing of the move being the surprise.

Ten-year bond yields dropped sharply on the initial announcement, brushing the 1980s-lows seen last week, but the rally soon lost its way with the reduction in official cash rates to 5.0 percent having been factored in for sometime.
"This was never going to be a rate cut that you were going to make a lot of money on," said one trader.
Analysts had generally expected the Reserve Bank to announce the rate cut after next week's board meeting, but once again the central bank caught the market on the hop.

"I think the particular timing had...to do with the Australian dollar having bounced overnight, and it meant they had an opportunity to cut and be sure the Australian dollar wouldn't go into freefall after the move," said Matthew Drennan, senior economist at Axiom Funds Management.
The local dollar saw an aggressive short squeeze in offshore trading, taking it to US$0.7500 at one stage, and subsequently held stable around the mid-US$0.7450s on the rate cut.

The RBA said the rate cut was based on the current inflation outlook and expected underlying inflation to remain below 2.0 percent going in 1998. It also said that wage pressure had subsided and that there was still scope for faster growth in output and growth.
The question now being asked in the market is whether this fifth rate cut within a year is the last.
David Bassanese, senior economist at Bankers Trust Australia, thinks it is likely to be the last at this stage.
"We think the RBA will want to get interest rates to a level where they don't have to change them for a year," he said.

"So they don't really want to get to a position where they go that one extra step, fearful that that may mean they would have to bring on a tightening earlier than they would otherwise like," he added. Other analysts said the RBA's statement was sufficiently open ended to suggest that they may ease again.

"Whether or not this is the last easing, we maintain our medium term bearish call for bonds, but beware, a spike to 6.25 percent for the 10-year bond and par on the spread to the U.S. could still occur," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia.
Citibank expects signs of stronger demand going into 1998 will lead the market to be concerned that this will spill over to higher inflation.
The local market outperformed the U.S. on the rate cut announcement, but failed to test last week's 25 basis point low.
